text:
I’ve spent some time reading the hundreds of replies to this post.

Apparently I’m a traitor. A cuck. A rape apologist. A fifth-column sympathiser. I should be deported. I should be put in the Tower. One charming fellow says, “We are going to hang you people, when we win.” Another asks why the military doesn’t attack the boat. Another says, “Just shoot it.”

All because I disputed Matt Goodwin’s claim that the British state was “locking down a large chunk of UK territory to facilitate the illegal migration invasion of our country.”

So after all the screaming, memes, threats and insults, let’s go back to what actually happened.

Hampshire Police were responding alongside the Maritime and Coastguard Agency, RNLI and Border Security Command to a small boat crossing. Officers were deployed both to ensure the emergency agencies could work safely and to manage the crowd gathering nearby. Once the people had been brought ashore, police say they were transported outside Hampshire for processing “as part of the normal process.”

That was the sinister operation.

Border authorities processing people who had crossed the border.

The police did impose restrictions. That bit is true. But contrary to some replies claiming this somehow proves the conspiracy, Section 34 is a statutory dispersal power used where police reasonably believe it may be necessary to reduce harassment, alarm, distress, crime, or disorder. Hampshire Police also imposed specific protest conditions under Section 14 and powers concerning face coverings. These were published, geographically defined and time-limited.

And what happened afterwards rather lessens the idea that the police invented the threat of disorder merely to protect “invaders”.

Twelve people were arrested.

The alleged offences included assaults on police officers, assaulting an emergency worker, affray, criminal damage, racially aggravated public-order offences, possession of a pyrotechnic article and obstructing a road used by ambulances. Officers themselves required treatment for injuries. Police subsequently described what occurred as violent public disorder, not peaceful protest.

So perhaps the police presence wasn't quite the inexplicable authoritarian outrage people were pretending it was.

Then there’s the apparent scandal of the RNLI and emergency services bringing people safely ashore.

They’re supposed to.

International maritime law requires assistance to people in distress at sea regardless of nationality, status or the circumstances in which they are found. Search-and-rescue arrangements exist to save human beings first and determine their immigration status afterwards.

That shouldn't be remotely controversial.

Yet look through these replies, and you find people asking why the boat wasn't attacked, demanding military action and treating rescue itself as treason.

Think about where the word “invasion” has taken them.
The next claim is that nothing is being done to stop these crossings.

Again, false.

The Government says French units operating under the latest UK-France arrangements prevented 185 small-boat events involving about 4,300 people in just the first three months, with 61% of attempted events prevented during that period. I can argue that enforcement should be stronger. What you can't honestly say is that nobody is trying to stop departures.

Nor are crossings endlessly soaring, as such timelines would have you believe. In the year ending June 2026, there were 33,374 small-boat arrivals, 23% fewer than the previous year. They continue to be a serious border problem. They are not an exponentially increasing invading army.

Then we get to the word that seems to have absolutely broken some people's brains:

Processed.

Apparently “processed” is now a sinister euphemism for “give them a free hotel and let them disappear into Britain forever.”

No.

The Home Office's own procedure says asylum screening involves photographing the claimant, taking fingerprints, interviewing them about who they are and where they came from, checking security and identity information, asking about criminality, recording their travel route and examining connections to third countries. Fingerprints can also be checked against police biometric records.

So to the bloke confidently telling me migrants can “tell Border Force any old shit”: congratulations, you've discovered why an immigration system doesn't rely solely on asking somebody their name and replying “fair enough mate, off you go.”

Processing is precisely the mechanism used to establish as much as reasonably possible about who somebody is and whether they have a legitimate claim.

And yes, these people are asylum seekers if they claim asylum.

That shouldn't require explaining, but apparently it does.

The Home Office says 95% of small-boat arrivals since 2018 have claimed asylum. Of the 178,845 small-boat arrivals who claimed asylum through the end of 2025, 132,894 had received a substantive initial decision by April 2026. 79,589 were granted protection or other leave, and 53,305 were refused. Another 33,413 claims had been withdrawn or received an administrative outcome.

You can dislike those grant rates. You can argue the criteria are too generous. You can campaign to change the law.

But “they aren't asylum seekers” is demonstrably wrong.

Likewise, “everyone gets to stay” is nonsense.

Across the entire asylum system in the year ending June 2026, there were 42,394 grants at initial decision and 73,478 refusals. The initial-decision grant rate was 38%.

If a claimant succeeds, they receive protection. If they don't qualify, the Government explicitly says they are asked to leave; after appeal rights are exhausted, they can leave voluntarily or be forcibly removed.

People are being removed, too.

In the year ending June 2026, more than 40,000 people returned to the UK, including 12,568 asylum-related returns. There were 3,310 returns of people who had arrived by small boat, up 35% on the previous year, and 9,694 small-boat arrivals had been returned since 2018.

Now cue someone shouting “THAT'S ONLY ABOUT 5%!”

Yes, if you divide cumulative small-boat returns by every arrival irrespective of the person's case, you can produce a small percentage.

But that's a completely useless denominator if you're trying to establish how many people who should have been removed actually were.

Your denominator includes recognised refugees with a legal right to remain, people whose claims are still being considered, people exercising appeal rights, people whose cases have been withdrawn, and people at different stages of the system.

You cannot simply label every person who hasn't been deported a failed deportation.

Several people were equally horrified to learn that asylum seekers aren't routinely imprisoned for months or years while their claims are decided.

Correct.

Asylum isn't a criminal sentence.

Home Office detention guidance explicitly says detention should be used sparingly and for the shortest period necessary. Claimants can instead be subject to reporting requirements, and failure to comply might result in a withdrawn claim or detention.

Apparently anything short of indefinite incarceration now counts as an open border.

Then there are the mythical riches.

One reply confidently describes free accommodation, mobile phones, credit plans, meal allowances and spending money.

Actual asylum support?

For somebody who qualifies because they would otherwise be destitute, the standard cash allowance is £49.18 per person per week. Where accommodation provides meals, it falls to £9.95 per week. They cannot simply choose where they live.

In June 2026, only 17% of people receiving asylum support were in hotels, and that number had halved over the previous year.

Again, debate whether taxpayers should provide that support. That's politics.

Just stop inventing a luxury lifestyle that doesn't exist.

Then there's “they're almost ALL young men.”

A kernel of truth is buried under the exaggeration: dangerous irregular routes disproportionately attract adult men. Official figures show that since 2018, 71% of detected illegal-route arrivals were adult men, while 18% were children.

So yes, most are adult men.

No, that does not mean almost everybody is a young man.

And male is not a synonym for rapist, terrorist or enemy soldier.

This brings me to the most grotesque distortion in the replies.

Someone posted the headline reporting Shabana Mahmood saying that nearly all women arriving by small boat have been raped, and triumphantly concluded that the Government was therefore importing their rapists.

Except that isn't what she said.

Mahmood was describing women being subjected to sexual violence and exploitation during their journeys, in the context of people traffickers exploiting vulnerable migrants. The article does not establish that the men travelling on whichever boat happens to arrive alongside them are the perpetrators.

They took a report about vulnerable women being raped and somehow transformed it into evidence that every unfamiliar brown man arriving in Britain is a rapist.

And then called everybody else dishonest.

Another reply asks whether I'll “accept personal responsibility” if anybody on the boat later commits terrorism or another serious crime.

No.

Why the fuck would I?

If somebody commits terrorism, the terrorist is responsible for terrorism. If authorities negligently miss information they reasonably ought to have identified, then those authorities can be held accountable for that failure.

Random citizens who support applying due process to asylum claims do not acquire collective responsibility for every future offence committed by anybody who ever claimed asylum.

That isn't justice. It's collective guilt

Then the rhetoric moves away from immigration entirely.

Mahmood and Khan are supposedly an “Islamic fifth column.” Mahmood should be “shipped to Pakistan”. Someone looks at Marble Arch and complains it isn't “English” enough anymore. Another says Europe has been conquered by “Islamic/Communism”. Somebody else posts that I must really be a “Mohamed” rather than a Gordon.

At that point nobody is discussing border policy.

They're discussing who counts as properly British.

And when someone in the replies confidently informs me that Hitler was actually far left, there isn't much mystery about the historical literacy we're dealing with either. The United States Holocaust Memorial Museum describes the Nazi Party as a radical far-right, racist, antisemitic, ultranationalist and anti-Marxist movement.

But what bothers me most in this thread isn't even the misinformation.

It's what happens after people accept it.

Look at the progression.

The migrants become “invaders”.
Emergency workers become collaborators.
Police become the enemy.
A democratic government becomes “treasonous”.
Muslim politicians become a “fifth column”.
Anyone challenging the story becomes a “traitor”.

And suddenly I have people telling me that “we are going to hang you people when we win”, talking about putting “traitors” in the Tower of London, advocating military action against a boat full of human beings and saying political opponents should be deported along with migrants.

That isn't ordinary disagreement about immigration policy.

Nor am I saying everyone who wants lower immigration is far right. That would be ridiculous.

You can want dramatically lower migration. You can oppose Channel crossings. You can demand quicker asylum decisions. You can want more removals. You can believe asylum law requires reform. You can believe hotels cost too much. You can peacefully protest every one of those things.

Millions of perfectly decent people will disagree on those questions.

But political disagreement can mutate into something else.

When migrants cease being individuals and become an invading mass.

When British Muslims become a fifth column.

When courts, police, rescuers and civil servants become collaborators.

When political opponents become traitors.

When ethnicity determines who really belongs.

When violence starts being discussed as patriotic necessity.

That is no longer a discussion about immigration numbers.

And this thread provides an extraordinary little case study in how people get there.

Somebody with an audience announces that the Government is facilitating an “invasion”.

People who already distrust the Government accept the premise.

Every ordinary part of border management then becomes supporting evidence. Police? Protecting the invasion. Coaches? Transporting the invasion. RNLI? Importing the invasion. Processing? Legalising the invasion. Dispersal orders after crowds assemble? Suppressing resistance to the invasion.

Contrary evidence can't penetrate the story because the institutions producing the evidence have already been incorporated into the conspiracy.

Government statistics? Lies.
Police statement? Cover-up.
Border Force procedure? Propaganda.
Journalists? Establishment.

Ask for evidence, and the response becomes “OPEN YOUR EYES, WE CAN SEE IT.”

That's not healthy scepticism.

It's a belief system designed so that nothing can ever disprove it.

One final thing, because I don't intend to make the same mistake as the people I'm criticising. This reply thread does not prove that Britain is full of millions of extremists or that civil war is around the corner. X is not Britain.

A viral reply section is not an opinion poll.

Ordinary people in that crowd will be genuinely worried about immigration, public services, housing, or social cohesion, and will have been persuaded that “invasion” accurately describes what is happening.

Those people should be argued with, not demonised.

But the people deliberately feeding them fantasies about treason, population replacement, secret government plots and enemy armies arriving on dinghies bear a much greater responsibility for where this rhetoric goes.

Because look at where some of their audience has already taken it.

Hanging. Shooting. Military action. Deporting political opponents. “Fifth columns”. “Traitors”.

And then, incredibly, these same people insist that they are defending British civilisation from hatred and extremism.

If your politics requires you to convince ordinary British people that frightened strangers on a sinking boat are enemy soldiers, that lifeboat crews are collaborators, that police officers are traitors. That fellow citizens who disagree with you deserve hanging, perhaps it's worth asking what you're supposedly saving Britain from, and what you're trying to turn Britain into.

That's the conversation we should be having.

And yes, this thread has far-right rhetoric.

I want to be precise about that, because “far right” shouldn't be thrown at everybody who wants immigration reduced. I’ll hold my hands up and say I’ve been guilty of that. To those for whom this holds, I’m genuinely sorry.

Wanting fewer small-boat crossings isn't inherently far right. Wanting stricter asylum rules isn't inherently far right. Wanting faster removals, lower immigration, or stronger border enforcement isn't inherently far right either.

That isn't what I'm identifying here.

I'm talking about the ideology plainly visible in parts of these replies.

The UK Government's own counter-extremism framework describes cultural nationalism as the belief that Western culture faces a fundamental threat from mass migration and particular ethnic or cultural groups, often accompanied by anti-Muslim hostility and anti-establishment conspiracy theories. It describes white/ethno-nationalism as treating migration and demographic change as an existential threat and sometimes advocating forced repatriation. 

ProtectUK also stresses that extreme-right activity is fragmented: people do not need to belong to some uniform organisation or wear a swastika before their rhetoric can draw from those ideas.

Now look at what actually appeared in this thread.

Britain is supposedly undergoing an “invasion”.
Islam has supposedly conquered Europe.
Muslim British politicians are a “fifth column”.
Shabana Mahmood should be sent to Pakistan.

London supposedly isn't properly British anymore because of the people living there.

Migrants are presented collectively as rapists, terrorists and enemy combatants.

The government, police, Border Force, the RNLI, and the media are depicted as collaborators in a deliberate national betrayal.

And anyone rejecting that worldview rapidly becomes a “traitor”, “quisling”, enemy or collaborator too.

Those themes aren't something I've projected onto the conversation. They are sitting there in black and white. And they map remarkably closely onto the cultural- and ethno-nationalist narratives British counter-extremism authorities actually describe: existential demographic threat, anti-Muslim hostility, conspiracy theories about establishment betrayal and hostility towards minorities regarded as insufficiently belonging.

Then comes the genuinely alarming part.

Somebody says, “We are going to hang you people, when we win.”

Another invokes the Tower of London for “traitors.”

Others suggest military action against the boat, say “just shoot it”, demand political opponents be deported alongside migrants, or talk about removing a “treasonous” government.

ProtectUK specifically distinguishes ordinary right-wing politics from extreme-right activity involving violence, and notes that political violence can emerge from cultural-nationalist, white-nationalist and white-supremacist milieus.

So no: not everybody in this thread is far right.

Some are plainly just angry. Some are badly informed about asylum law. Some have believed sensationalist claims. Some are simply throwing playground abuse around.

But pretending there is no far-right current running through this thread would require ignoring what people are actually saying.

And that matters because you can watch the radicalising logic unfold almost line by line.

First you're told there is an invasion.

If it's an invasion, the people arriving become the enemy.
If they're the enemy, the people rescuing them become collaborators.
If the Government processes them, the Government becomes treasonous.
If the police prevent a crowd from interfering, the police become agents of the enemy.
If a British Muslim politician administers the system, they're a fifth columnist.
If another British citizen objects to any of this, they're a traitor too.

And once you've reached that point, hanging traitors, shooting boats and using military force no longer sound monstrous to somebody inside the narrative. They begin to sound like logical responses to the emergency they've been persuaded exists.

That's why the word “invasion” matters.

It's not merely colourful language for “immigration levels I think are too high.” It changes the moral framework entirely. An immigration problem calls for policy. An invasion calls for enemies, collaborators, resistance and ultimately force.

And that is exactly the vocabulary this thread descended into.

The most important distinction therefore isn't left versus right.

It's between people who want to argue democratically about immigration policy and people being drawn into a worldview in which whole groups become enemies, institutions become traitors, and violence becomes patriotic.

Britain can have an extremely tough argument about immigration without doing that. We can radically reduce immigration if voters choose governments promising it. We can rewrite asylum law within the constraints Britain decides to retain. We can remove people who have no right to remain. We can demand competence from Border Force and accountability from government.

None of that requires convincing ourselves that our Muslim neighbours constitute a fifth column, that lifeboat crews are assisting an enemy army, or that fellow citizens deserves the rope because they disagree with us.

And that's ultimately what this thread exposes.

Not simply misinformation about one boat in Gosport, but the machinery by which misinformation becomes grievance, grievance becomes conspiracy, conspiracy becomes dehumanisation, and dehumanisation can make genuinely authoritarian and violent ideas seem acceptable.

So when I call out the far-right element here, I'm not talking about everyone who wants fewer migrants.

I'm talking about the people telling us Britain is being ethnically or culturally conquered, that Muslim Britons are an enemy within, that democratic institutions are committing treason, and that the appropriate response is force against migrants and punishment for their political opponents.

If that isn't the politics you believe in, good.

Then don't let people who do believe it convince you that they're merely speaking on your behalf about immigration.

text:
Statement : The removal of BitChat from the India App Store is unconstitutional. Section 69A permits the blocking of unlawful information, not of a messenger for working during internet shutdowns.

New Delhi, 3 October 2026

An Apple App Review notice published today by Jack Dorsey on X records that BitChat has been removed from the India App Store "per demand from the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology", issued under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, on the ground that the application "includes content that is illegal in India". The notice adds that BitChat's TestFlight builds are no longer available for testing in India. It does not identify the content said to be illegal or the ground under Section 69A invoked. The blocking order has not been published. The Internet Freedom Foundation condemns the order and calls for its immediate publication and withdrawal.

BitChat relays end-to-end encrypted messages between nearby phones over Bluetooth mesh. It has no servers and hosts no content of its own. What travels through it is the private speech of its users, so the claim that the application "includes" illegal content is incoherent. The State's actual objection stands recorded in the notices the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre issued on 23 July 2026 to GitHub, Google and Apple against BitChat, Briar and Bridgefy which stated that such applications work even during internet shutdowns and hamper lawful interception, attribution and traceability. Those notices, issued under Section 79(3)(b) were reportedly withdrawn after public disclosure. The same end has now been pursued through Section 69A. The objection is to capability of an application, not to content it transmits. A citizen's ability to speak to another citizen while the State has switched the internet off is not a ground of restriction under Section 69A or Article 19(2) of the Constitution.

Section 69A survived constitutional scrutiny in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) because of its safeguards which included the need for a reasoned, recorded order, committee review, and a hearing to the originator under Rule 8 of the Blocking Rules, 2009, which the Delhi High Court enforced in Tanul Thakur v. Union of India (2022). Further, Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) requires that orders restricting fundamental rights be published and adopt the least restrictive measure. However, it appears in this instance, each safeguard has been evaded. A secret order blocking an entire application, rather than any identified unlawful information, is the most restrictive and disproprotionate measure available. Further, the confidentiality claimed under Rule 16 cannot defeat the right to challenge an order, and the constitutionality of this blocking regime is itself pending consideration before the Supreme Court.

While removal from the App Store does not delete BitChat from phones, it stops new downloads and security updates, leaving existing users on unpatched versions, and it ends security testing in India through TestFlight. During the Jantar Mantar protests, when mobile internet was suspended and jammers were deployed, Bluetooth mesh messaging was a channel of last resort through which young people coordinated their safety. To our knowledge, Apple has removed BitChat on a government's demand in only one other country. This is in China, in April this year.

Our demands

1. MeitY must publish the blocking order, the ground invoked and the record of the committee's proceedings, and serve the developers with a copy and an opportunity of hearing.

2. The direction must be withdrawn. Any specific unlawful use must be met with targeted proceedings under due process, not the removal of a communications tool for everyone.

3. Apple must disclose the demand in its transparency reporting and notify its users in India, and must state whether parallel directions have been received in respect of other app stores.

4. The secrecy of the blocking regime must end. The Blocking Rules, 2009 should be amended to require publication of orders and notice to originators, without awaiting the outcome of the pending constitutional challenge.

The Internet Freedom Foundation will file applications under the Right to Information Act seeking a copy of the order, and stands ready to assist the developers and affected users in India.

text:
Statement: IFF condemns the internet shutdown in Connaught Place ahead of today's protest. We are tracing the suspension order.

New Delhi, 2 October 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the suspension of mobile internet services in and around Connaught Place, New Delhi, this morning. At 9:40 am, Jio subscribers in the area received a message stating: "As per government instructions Internet services have been stopped in your area till further notice." The shutdown took effect before a protest called for 11 am at Jantar Mantar, seeking the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner, had even begun. 

Delhi Police has refused permission for the gathering, prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 are in force across New Delhi district, and entry and exit at eleven metro stations have been closed. On Gandhi Jayanti, the answer to a call for protest in the capital has been to switch off the internet for everyone who lives, works, trades and reports in its centre. We call for the immediate restoration of services. 

At the time of release of this statement, we have not been able to locate any suspension order published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. The public does not know who directed this shutdown, on what grounds, over what area, or until when. IFF is attempting to trace the order and will make it public as soon as we obtain a copy.

In Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637, the Supreme Court held that speech and trade over the internet are protected under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution, and that every suspension order must be published, reasoned, proportionate and limited in time. Under Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023 and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, only the Union or State Home Secretary may issue such an order, for reasons recorded in writing. The order must be published and must specify the area, the services and a fixed duration and it may be passed only where no other reasonable means would serve. A shutdown announced to subscribers as lasting "till further notice", imposed before a single person had assembled, cannot be squared with these safeguards. It follows repeated suspensions around Jantar Mantar in July 2026. Switching off the network is becoming a routine response to protest in the national capital. IFF condemns the internet shutdown in parts of Central Delhi. 

We call upon the Government of India and the Government of NCT of Delhi to:

1. Immediately restore mobile internet services in Connaught Place and all affected parts of Central Delhi.

2. Publish the suspension order forthwith, together with the reasons recorded in writing.

3. Disclose the issuing authority, the precise areas and services covered, and the period of operation.

4. Place the order before the Review Committee within five days, as the Rules require, and make its findings public.

text:
The Delhi Police's takedown drive against posts critical of the Prime Minister is unconstitutional. 

New Delhi, 27 July 2026

Media reports today state that the Delhi Police has directed social media platforms to remove posts, videos, memes and reels containing remarks it describes as "abusive", "offensive" and "objectionable" towards the Prime Minister, uploaded during the student protests at Jantar Mantar and after the 'Sansad Chalo' march of 20 July 2026. At least three platforms have reportedly received notices. Several posts have already been taken down. A dedicated police team is monitoring social media to identify further content, and reports indicate that criminal proceedings are contemplated against those who posted it. No order has been published. While reports indicate the notices invoke the Information Technology Act, the specific provision relied upon and the text of the notices remain undisclosed. 

The Internet Freedom Foundation condemns this takedown drive and calls for the notices to be disclosed and withdrawn.

On the reports available, the content being removed is political expression. The movement at Jantar Mantar has been conducted as much through reels, memes, posters and digital artwork as through assembly on the ground. This is how a digital native generation raised online speaks about accountability. As per Article 19(2) restrictions on speech only on eight specified grounds. Offensiveness is not one of them. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, the Supreme Court struck down Section 66A of the IT Act precisely because expressions such as "grossly offensive" and causing "annoyance" were vague, subjective, and swept protected speech within their net. Eleven years later, the Delhi Police is applying the same standard through informal notices and legal powers which are not being publicly disclosed. 

As per existing practices there are two routes for removing online content. The first is Section 69A of the IT Act read with the Blocking Rules, 2009, which requires a reasoned order, committee review, and notice to the originator, as the Delhi High Court affirmed in Tanul Thakur v. Union of India (2022). The second is Section 79(3)(b), which Shreya Singhal read down to require a court order or a government notification strictly confined to Article 19(2) grounds. If these notices were routed through the Sahyog Portal, they rest on a regime whose constitutionality remains under challenge before multiple High Courts. However, even if it is used police notices citing offensiveness satisfy neither. 

Reports that platforms were told the content violates "their policies" make the defect worse, the police have no mandate to enforce the community guidelines of private companies. Unpublished directions are also contrary to Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) 3 SCC 637, which requires that orders restricting fundamental rights be published so that they can be challenged. If the underlying theory is defamation of the Prime Minister, the police have no role at all. Defamation under Section 356 of the BNS is a non-cognizable offence, prosecuted only on a complaint by the person aggrieved under Section 222 of the BNSS. 

Our demands

1. The Delhi Police must publish every notice issued, the legal provision invoked, and the list of URLs affected.

2. Notices directed at satire, criticism, and political commentary must be withdrawn. Any removal must follow the procedures under Section 69A or a judicial order.

3. No criminal proceedings should be initiated against persons for speech that does not meet the constitutional threshold of incitement.

4. Platforms must decline requests unsupported by valid legal orders, notify affected users, and disclose the number of government demands in their transparency reports.

Students who question an examination system are exercising their fundamental rights and deleting their posts will not delete their questions.

Reports referred to:

1. Times of India, "Delhi Police orders removal of offensive posts against PM Narendra Modi linked to NEET paper leak protests", 27 July 2026
2. News18, "Delhi Police Issues Notices To Social Media Platforms Over Offensive Posts Against PM Modi During Jantar Mantar Protest", 27 July 2026

I have my twitter back. 

It took me 6 days, a cyber police complaint and a legal notice to twitter to recover my account. 

If you got a DM from me last week asking you to vote for me for a podcast, that was not me. Please don't click it & If you already did, please change your password ASAP.

Here's what happened:

→I received a late night DM from a friend to vote on a podcast which redirected me to a a login page that looked right, and I typed in my password (classic)

→The attacker logged in and changed my 2FA within minutes & I was locked out of my account. (I still don't understand how my email and phone number were changed. Neither my email nor my phone was compromised.)

→Then he used account to DM followers a fake "vote for me" link. Each person who clicks becomes the next account sending it. That is how these spread.

What didn't work:

→ I filed X's hacked account form within the hour. Less than two hours later, the reply came: X could not verify me as the account owner. Their suggestion was to create a new account. Once 2FA is changed, the automated system treats the attacker as the real owner.

→ So I went to the Grievance Officer. Under the IT Rules, 2021, X must appoint a Resident Grievance Officer in India. He has no email address. X does not accept legal notices by email. 

The only options are a web form or post to their physical office.

Here's what worked:

→First, a cyber complaint on https://t.co/Uzds8BObDW (or call 1930).

→Second, a legal notice to the Grievance Officer. Under the IT Rules, impersonation complaints must be acted on within 24 hours.

→Third, the same notice sent by registered post, and to every X email address I could find.

The notice put X on record. It set out the ticket number, the phishing link, and the cyber complaint number. It showed proof of ownership: the registered email, the phone number, and the Premium subscription paid from my card. It ended with a clear ask and a deadline.

Six days after the hack, I was back in.

If this happens to you:
• Act within hours
• File X's hacked account form from your registered email and be persistent (this is important)
• File at https://t.co/Uzds8BObDW and keep the acknowledgement
• Notice to the Grievance Officer via the https://t.co/YkDfcMQwzE form and by post

🗳️ AP LOCAL BODY POLLS | SEC gears up for two-phase election plan
The Andhra Pradesh State Election Commission (SEC) has stepped up preparations for the long-pending rural and urban local body elections, with officials being told to remain ready to begin the poll process at short notice.

State Election Commissioner Anil Chandra Punetha held a three-hour review with district collectors, SPs, police commissioners and senior officials on October 8, directing them to keep manpower, security and election logistics ready once the remaining legal and administrative issues are cleared.

🔹 Two-phase election plan

According to a Times of India report, the SEC has prepared a two-phase strategy aimed at completing the local body election process by December 2026.

The proposed structure reportedly includes:

Phase 1: Elections to 59 Urban Local Bodies

Phase 2: Elections to the remaining urban bodies along with rural local bodies, including thousands of gram panchayats and wards across Andhra Pradesh.

The SEC has already finalised polling-station lists for 59 ULBs, including 58 municipalities/nagar panchayats and the Vizianagaram Municipal Corporation, indicating that a significant portion of the groundwork is complete.

⚖️ BC reservations remain the biggest legal question

The election process is closely linked to the continuing dispute over 34% reservation for Backward Classes in local bodies.

On October 1, the Andhra Pradesh High Court struck down the government orders providing 34% BC reservation, holding that the combined SC, ST and BC reservation crossed the 50% ceiling without the required empirical exercise. The court also directed the government and SEC to move ahead with the election process within six weeks.

The matter has since reached the Supreme Court, where related petitions are being considered.

Until there is greater legal clarity on reservations, final seat-wise reservation and candidate calculations remain a key unresolved factor.

💰 Why the elections are financially important

The elections are not only politically significant.

The Andhra Pradesh government has said that delays could affect access to Finance Commission grants for local bodies.

Earlier cabinet-level discussions identified around ₹3,862 crore in 16th Finance Commission-linked grants — including approximately ₹2,300 crore for rural local bodies and ₹1,562 crore for urban bodies — as funds that could be affected if elected bodies are not constituted in time.

That makes the poll calendar important not just for political representation, but also for local infrastructure and municipal finances.

🏛️ Political parties already preparing

The ruling NDA alliance has simultaneously intensified its political preparations.

Chief Minister N. Chandrababu Naidu and Deputy Chief Minister Pawan Kalyan recently held discussions on seat-sharing, candidate selection and coordination between TDP and Jana Sena ahead of the polls.

TDP leaders have also said that multiple rounds of seat-sharing discussions have already taken place, though final allocations remain linked to the reservation matrix.

🔎 What happens next?

The election machinery appears increasingly ready.

The real triggers now are:

• final legal clarity on BC reservations
• formal SEC notification
• finalisation of reservation rosters
• candidate selection and alliance seat-sharing
• deployment of election personnel and security

Dear @CoinDCX Team,Ceo @smtgpt 

I am writing to raise a very serious concern regarding my recent withdrawal from CoinDCX.

=> Last month, I placed a withdrawal request (under $1000 USDT) from CoinDCX to my SBI Bank account. 3. What is the meaning of a P2P exchange if, after tax deduction, withdrawals are still blocked by banks and flagged by authorities?

—> If this problem is not addressed with a clear and transparent solution, then users will be forced to assume that CoinDCX’s P2P services are unsafe or misleading.

I request an urgent clarification from your team or leadership regarding this matter.

Dear @raghav_chadha ,

I know you are doing very well in Parliament by raising small issues that were ignored by most Members of Parliament but have a bigger impact.

I am writing this post regarding an account lien and bank freeze by the Cyber Police of India.

In my case, the issue started when I received a message from my bank branch stating that my account had received a police notice of lien of 6000 rupees. I immediately went to my bank branch and asked them why my account had a lien of 6000 rupees. They followed some procedure and gave me a printout which contained the acknowledgement of my lien. One of the bank employees told me that I should contact the cyber police mentioned on the paper and provide them with the details of the 6000 rupees, such as where it came from and for what reason. However, they did not give me any specific reason why my bank account had received the lien.

Later, I checked my bank statement to find the details of the 6000 rupees transaction and noticed that my case was reported on 6 December 2025, and I had received a transaction of 6000 rupees on the same date. I remember that my neighbour had sent me this 6000 rupees and asked me to withdraw it from the ATM because he had an urgent situation as his mother was going to her village due to an emergency. As a friend, I withdrew the money and gave it to him.

Now I have all the proofs and details to explain to the police, so I emailed all the details to the Bangalore Cyber Cell or the police station where my notice was issued, as mentioned in the acknowledgement given by my bank. However, I did not receive any response. I then tried to contact the investigation officer mentioned in the report. I called several times, keeping a gap of five to six hours out of respect for his time and duties, as they may have many other responsibilities. I also sent him a message on WhatsApp, but there was still no response.

After four to five days, I called again, and this time he picked up the call. He was speaking in the local language, which I did not understand, as I am from Maharashtra and not familiar with the local language of Bangalore. I then started speaking in English, and he told me that I have to come to Bangalore and verify my documents. I explained that for 6000 rupees, it would not be beneficial for me to travel to Bangalore because transportation, food, and stay would cost more than 6000 rupees. He said that he does not know and that I have to come, otherwise he will not issue the No Objection Certificate, and then he ended the call.

This issue may look small, but similar issues are happening everywhere, and no one is noticing them. It feels like “Kare koi aur bhare koi.” Many innocent people face this issue, and it remains unresolved. Because of chain transactions that come into accounts, some people are unable to use their own money. If I travel, I will have to spend more than 6000 rupees to remove the lien. I believe this issue can be resolved through email or online verification, but the investigation officer denied it.

I am also tagging Pushpendra Sir @pushpendrakum and Bangalore Cyber Police @BlrCityPolice . If you could please look into this matter.

Thank you.

🚨 Binance P2P se Bank Account Freeze? Poori Guide + Real Solution (2026)

Bhai aur beheno, agar aap bhi Binance P2P trading karte ho aur suddenly bank account freeze ho gaya hai toh pareshan mat ho. Yeh bahut common problem hai India mein. Innocent log bhi fas jaate hain jab kisi buyer/seller ka paisa kisi fraud case se link hota hai.

Yeh steps follow karo - 

1️⃣ Sabse Pehle Bank Branch Jaao  
   - Freeze ka exact reason, Cyber Crime complaint number, IO naam aur Police Station details lo.  
   - Written notice maang lo.

2️⃣ Saare Proofs Collect Karo (Bahut Important)  
   - Binance P2P complete order history (screenshots)  
   - Buyer/Seller ke saath chat  
   - Payment proof (UPI, bank transfer screenshot)  
   - Bank statement jisme transaction dikhe  
   - Aadhaar, PAN, Binance account details

3️⃣ Binance Support ko turant contact karo  
   - App mein Help section → Submit ticket  
   - Order ID aur proofs attach karo. Woh counterparty ko investigate kar sakte hain.

4️⃣ Cyber Cell mein Representation Daalo  
   - Local Cyber Police Station ya online portal pe jaao.  
   - Detailed application likho ki transaction genuine tha Binance P2P pe hua.  
   - Saare proofs attach karo.  
   - Lawyer (Cyber crime specialist) ki madad le lo - yeh bahut kaam aata hai.

5️⃣ Follow-up karte raho  
   - Har 7-10 din mein bank aur cyber cell ko call/email karo.  
   - Partial release ke liye request kar sakte ho.

Extra Tips jo future mein bacha sakte hain:
• P2P ke liye alag dedicated bank account use karo (savings account mat use karo)
• Sirf verified buyers/sellers ke saath trade karo
• Video verification ya proper KYC maango
• Bahut bade amounts ek baar mein mat trade karo
• Binance P2P risky hai India mein, agar ho sake toh avoid karo

quotedTweet.text:
Statement : The removal of BitChat from the India App Store is unconstitutional. Section 69A permits the blocking of unlawful information, not of a messenger for working during internet shutdowns.

New Delhi, 3 October 2026

An Apple App Review notice published today by Jack Dorsey on X records that BitChat has been removed from the India App Store "per demand from the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology", issued under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, on the ground that the application "includes content that is illegal in India". The notice adds that BitChat's TestFlight builds are no longer available for testing in India. It does not identify the content said to be illegal or the ground under Section 69A invoked. The blocking order has not been published. The Internet Freedom Foundation condemns the order and calls for its immediate publication and withdrawal.

BitChat relays end-to-end encrypted messages between nearby phones over Bluetooth mesh. It has no servers and hosts no content of its own. What travels through it is the private speech of its users, so the claim that the application "includes" illegal content is incoherent. The State's actual objection stands recorded in the notices the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre issued on 23 July 2026 to GitHub, Google and Apple against BitChat, Briar and Bridgefy which stated that such applications work even during internet shutdowns and hamper lawful interception, attribution and traceability. Those notices, issued under Section 79(3)(b) were reportedly withdrawn after public disclosure. The same end has now been pursued through Section 69A. The objection is to capability of an application, not to content it transmits. A citizen's ability to speak to another citizen while the State has switched the internet off is not a ground of restriction under Section 69A or Article 19(2) of the Constitution.

Section 69A survived constitutional scrutiny in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) because of its safeguards which included the need for a reasoned, recorded order, committee review, and a hearing to the originator under Rule 8 of the Blocking Rules, 2009, which the Delhi High Court enforced in Tanul Thakur v. Union of India (2022). Further, Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) requires that orders restricting fundamental rights be published and adopt the least restrictive measure. However, it appears in this instance, each safeguard has been evaded. A secret order blocking an entire application, rather than any identified unlawful information, is the most restrictive and disproprotionate measure available. Further, the confidentiality claimed under Rule 16 cannot defeat the right to challenge an order, and the constitutionality of this blocking regime is itself pending consideration before the Supreme Court.

While removal from the App Store does not delete BitChat from phones, it stops new downloads and security updates, leaving existing users on unpatched versions, and it ends security testing in India through TestFlight. During the Jantar Mantar protests, when mobile internet was suspended and jammers were deployed, Bluetooth mesh messaging was a channel of last resort through which young people coordinated their safety. To our knowledge, Apple has removed BitChat on a government's demand in only one other country. This is in China, in April this year.

Our demands

1. MeitY must publish the blocking order, the ground invoked and the record of the committee's proceedings, and serve the developers with a copy and an opportunity of hearing.

2. The direction must be withdrawn. Any specific unlawful use must be met with targeted proceedings under due process, not the removal of a communications tool for everyone.

3. Apple must disclose the demand in its transparency reporting and notify its users in India, and must state whether parallel directions have been received in respect of other app stores.

4. The secrecy of the blocking regime must end. The Blocking Rules, 2009 should be amended to require publication of orders and notice to originators, without awaiting the outcome of the pending constitutional challenge.

The Internet Freedom Foundation will file applications under the Right to Information Act seeking a copy of the order, and stands ready to assist the developers and affected users in India.
